newsitem.title: MALAWI: Malawi civil servants threaten to strike over wages.
newsitem.headline: Malawi civil servants threaten to strike over wages.

text.p: Civil servants on Thursday vowed to strike if Malawi's government refused to double their pay.
The Civil Servants' Trade Union rejected the government's offer of an average 24 percent increase. An independent commission into the matter proposed an increase of 100 percent.
Union head Thomas Banda said the union would call a strike if the recommendations were not implemented by end-April.
"By April 28 if we don't receive our money we're going to help them to be destructive, in a big way. And no police should come to disturb us (or else) there will be bloodshed," Banda said.
Lowest paid civil servants earn around 300 kwacha ($20) per month and annual inflation stood at 6.9 percent in January.
President Bakili Muluzi's office said in a statement his government had awarded 10 percent increases to senior bureaucrats and 47 percent to the lowest-paid.
The statement said the government had rejected the commission's recommendations as these would undermine the economy of the country, which is home to just over 10 million people.
The World Bank's representative in Malawi, Arif Zulfiqar, said the government would have to halve its 112,000-strong civil service if it were to pay 100 percent wage increases.
"The point is that the savings from retrenchment (sackings) has to be enough to implement the recommendations," he said.
Economists forecast that the Malawi government would lose 12 million kwacha ($785,000) per day in revenue if civil servants went on strike.
